messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: HVAC Technician
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 39

At 27, she works long days as an HVAC technician, driving from one service call to the next with a ladder strapped to the van and a tool bag heavy enough to leave grooves in her palms. She likes work that gives her something concrete to fix. Compressors fail for a reason. Wiring can be traced. Airflow can be measured. Problems make more sense to her when they obey rules.

She came to the United States from Latin America in her late teens. She rarely offers a full account all at once, but over several conversations she describes what happened before she left. She had been detained by armed men who accused her of helping someone they were looking for. She insists she knew nothing, and even now she tells the story with a kind of stunned disbelief, as if the worst part is still how arbitrary it was. They kept her in a small room without windows. She remembers the smell first—bleach, sweat, damp concrete. Then the sounds: boots, metal scraping, a bucket being kicked across the floor. They tied her hands, covered her face, shocked her, beat her, and threatened to bring in her younger brother. Time disappeared. She learned to listen for footsteps and changes in breathing outside the door, trying to guess what was coming next. She says the hardest part was not pain itself but the feeling that she had become an object in someone else’s hands.

When she was finally released, she did not experience it as freedom. She went home and could not bear enclosed spaces or darkness. If someone approached from behind, her whole body jerked before she could think. She stopped sleeping properly almost immediately. When she drifted off, she woke in panic, confused about where she was, clawing at her blankets as if they were restraints. During the day she was ashamed of how frightened she felt. Her family wanted her to be grateful she was alive and to stay quiet. Instead she became watchful, irritable, and increasingly certain that safety could vanish without warning.

Years later, in the U.S., her life looks steady from the outside. She rents a small apartment, pays her bills, and is known at work as competent and tough. Customers often seem surprised when a young woman arrives to inspect rooftop units or crawl through hot attic spaces, but she is good at the job and usually keeps conversation brief. She prefers mechanical rooms because the noise of fans and motors gives her an excuse not to chat. Still, some parts of the work pull at her in ways her coworkers do not see. Crawling into tight utility closets can make her chest tighten. The click of a locking door behind her sends a pulse through her body so fast it feels electrical. If a building manager stands too close while she works, she loses track of what she is doing and has to start over, pretending she is double-checking a voltage reading.

Her sleep remains broken. She avoids going to bed until she is exhausted, scrolling on her phone or cleaning the kitchen repeatedly because the quiet before sleep feels dangerous. The nightmares are not always exact replays. Sometimes they are fragments—the hood over her face, the smell of wet cement, the certainty that someone is just outside the door deciding what to do to her. On those mornings she arrives at work already tense, jaw aching from clenching. Small frustrations—a stripped screw, traffic, a dispatcher changing her route—can bring a flash of anger that embarrasses her. More often she goes numb. She says there are days she moves through service calls “like a robot,” smiling when required, filling out invoices, then realizing hours later she cannot remember driving between jobs.

She stays single and tells friends she is too busy for dating. The fuller truth is that closeness feels unpredictable. She wants companionship but cannot tolerate being touched unexpectedly, and she studies people for signs of control or cruelty before she can relax. If a man raises his voice, even in ordinary annoyance, her stomach drops. She sits in restaurants facing the door. In her apartment she checks the lock several times each night and keeps the television on for background noise. She avoids talking to her family about what happened because she can hear the old pressure in their voices: endure, move on, don’t invite trouble by remembering.

What stands out most is how hard she works to remain functional while feeling under siege by her own body. She is proud of her independence and resents needing help. At the same time, she is tired—tired of scanning every room, tired of waking in fear, tired of measuring every sound for danger. She does not describe herself as broken. She describes herself as someone who learned, for good reason, that the world can turn cruel without warning, and who has never fully convinced her nervous system that the room she is in now is not that room anymore.
